parts.title: Multiple choice (Questions 1–50)
parts.instructions: This paper has 50 multiple-choice questions (1 to 50). Each question has 4 choices. Choose ONE best answer and blacken its letter on the separate answer sheet. Sections: A. Dialogue (1–4), B. Grammar and vocabulary (5–34), C. Table (35–40), D. Reading passage (41–50).

source.notes: Transcribed from the PDF text layer of Version A and checked against the page images. Bold words (e.g. they, the same thing, decorate in the passage; not/false in stems) are plain text here; there is no underlining. V-B has the same questions, reordered, with options shuffled.

Passage line 11 ‘It never uses them for smelling’ (them = its nose; should be ‘it’). Passage line numbers 5–25 shown as [line N].

passages.title: Dialogue between a visitor and a secretary
passages.instructions: Complete the dialogue between a visitor and a secretary. Choose the secretary’s correct answers from the choices given (A–D).
paragraphs: Visitor: Please, I want to see the manager.
Secretary: ______ (1)
Visitor: Can I see her tomorrow morning?
Secretary: ______ (2)
Visitor: Can I leave a message, please?
Secretary: ______ (3)
Visitor: Would you please give me your phone number?
Secretary: ______ (4)
Choices given: A. Of course, you can.  B. Here you are.  C. I’m sorry. She’s just left.  D. No. We don’t open on Saturdays.

passages.title: Dolphins
passages.instructions: Read the story and answer the questions (41–50) according to the information in the story.
paragraphs: Dolphins are not fish, but warm blooded mammals. Like all other mammals, dolphins have lungs. Mammals, unlike fish, feed their young with milk that is produced in the mother’s body.

Dolphins live in groups, and speak to each other in their own language. In this they are [line 5] like other animals, such as bees and birds. But dolphins are very different from almost all land animals. Their brain is nearly the same size as our own, and they live a long time - at least twenty or thirty years.
Dolphins seem to like man, and for thousands of years there have been stories about the dolphin and its friendship with people.

[line 10] A dolphin has teeth, it eats fish, and its young are born alive. It can grow up to three and a half meters in length. Its nose is very long and forms a beak. It never uses them for smelling because it has no sense of smell.

Like some animals dolphins use sounds to help them find their way. They make these sounds to talk to each other and to help them find food. We now know they do not use [line 15] their ears to receive these sounds, but the lower part of the mouth called the jaw.

People have known about these animals for a long time. In about 70 BCE, Pliny, the Roman writer, wrote about the way dolphins helped fishermen catch fish. Today, there are stories about the same thing on the west coast of Africa.

Some dolphins seem to look for people. They leave the others and come into our harbours [line 20] and swim up and down near the beaches. There are stories of dolphins mixing with swimmers, and of children riding on their backs.
Today, some people continue to kill dolphins, but many countries of the world now protect them and in these places it’s against the law to kill them.

Eritrea has many different species of dolphin. People call them Abu Salama to show that [line 25] they are peaceful animals. There are hotels, restaurants, shops etc by their names. We also decorate our walls with pictures of dolphins. We love and take care of them very much.
passages.note: Line numbers (5–25) as printed in the margin. Bold in the paper: they (line 4), the same thing (line 18), decorate (line 26).

questions.stem: Dialogue, gap (1). Visitor: “Please, I want to see the manager.” Secretary: “______” Visitor: “Can I see her tomorrow morning?”

options.D: No. We don’t open on Saturdays.

explanation_steps: The visitor then asks to see the manager tomorrow. So she cannot see her now.
“I’m sorry. She’s just left.” explains why.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 1 (p. 1–21): conversations.
questions.explain_simple: The manager is not there now: “She’s just left.”
tips: The next line (“Can I see her tomorrow?”) shows the manager is not there.

options.D: No. We don’t open on Saturdays.

questions.stem: The ostrich has the ______ neck of all other birds.
explanation_steps: “the … of all birds” → superlative.
Short adjective long → the longest.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 58; English Grade 7, p. 16, 124; English Grade 8, p. 109.
questions.explain_simple: One bird compared with all birds → the longest.
tips: the + adjective-est + of all.

similar_questions.stem: The giraffe is the ______ animal of all.
explanation_steps: the tallest.

textbook_ref.rule: Long adjectives: more ... than / the most ...; short adjectives: -er than / the -est. 'not as ... as' means 'less ... than'.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 58; English Grade 7, p. 16, 124; English Grade 8, p. 109

questions.review_flag: Minor wording error: ‘of all other birds’ should be ‘of all birds’. The answer is still C.

questions.stem: What is the opposite of top?
explanation_steps: top ↔ bottom (the highest part ↔ the lowest part).
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 222; English Grade 8, p. 160.
questions.explain_simple: The opposite of top is bottom.
tips: top–bottom, high–low, up–down.

similar_questions.stem: What is the opposite of front?
explanation_steps: front ↔ back.

textbook_ref.topic: Opposites and words with the same meaning
textbook_ref.rule: A synonym has the same meaning (hit = strike); an opposite has the reverse meaning (happy – sad).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 222; English Grade 8, p. 160

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is correct?

options.A: Dolphins are most friendly animals in the sea.
options.B: Dolphins are the more friendly animals in the sea.
options.C: Dolphins are the most friendly animals in the sea.
options.D: Dolphins are the more friendly animals in the sea.

explanation_steps: “in the sea” compares dolphins with all sea animals → superlative: the most friendly.
A misses “the”; B and D use the comparative “more” without “than”.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 58; English Grade 7, p. 16, 124; English Grade 8, p. 109.
questions.explain_simple: the most friendly animals in the sea.
tips: Superlative needs “the”.

similar_questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?

options.A: Gold is the most expensive metal here.
options.B: Gold is most expensive metal here.
options.C: Gold is the more expensive metal here.

textbook_ref.rule: Long adjectives: more ... than / the most ...; short adjectives: -er than / the -est. 'not as ... as' means 'less ... than'.

questions.stem: Does she drive a car?
explanation_steps: “Does she …?” → Yes, she does / No, she doesn’t.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 100–101.
questions.explain_simple: “Does she …?” → “Yes, she does.”
tips: Yes + does; No + doesn’t.

similar_questions.stem: Does your father smoke?
explanation_steps: No, he doesn’t.

questions.stem: Look at ______ hyena! It is running after the donkey.
explanation_steps: The speaker points to one hyena that both people can see now.
A thing we both know/see takes “the”. Also “hyena” starts with a consonant sound, so “an” is wrong.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 74; English Grade 8, p. 56–58, 204.
questions.explain_simple: We can both see the hyena. So: the hyena.
tips: Use “the” for a thing the listener can see or knows.

similar_questions.stem: Look at ______ bird on the roof!
explanation_steps: The bird we can see → the.

textbook_ref.rule: Use 'the' for a thing that is the only one (the moon, the sun) or already known; a/an for one thing that is not specific.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 74; English Grade 8, p. 56–58, 204

questions.stem: Our teacher is a very hardworking person. The school gave ______ a prize.
explanation_steps: We do not know if the teacher is a man or a woman.
So “him” and “her” are both possible → A and B.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 61; English Grade 7, p. 7–8.
questions.explain_simple: The teacher can be a man or a woman. So “him” or “her”.
tips: No clue about man or woman? Both him and her can be right.

similar_questions.stem: My doctor is very kind. Everybody likes ______.
explanation_steps: The doctor can be a man or a woman.

textbook_ref.rule: Use an object pronoun (me, him, her, us, them) after a verb or preposition; possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs) replace a noun.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 61; English Grade 7, p. 7–8

questions.review_flag: The item depends on ‘teacher’ being either sex, so D ‘A and B’ is the intended answer; a student who picks A or B is not using wrong grammar. Teacher decision.

questions.stem: How ______ books did you buy yesterday? And how ______ did you pay?
explanation_steps: books can be counted → how many books.
“How much did you pay?” asks about money (an amount) → much.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 148, 274–276; English Grade 8, Units 6–7.
questions.explain_simple: books → many; money → how much.
tips: How much …? is used for price/money.

similar_questions.stem: How ______ pens do you have? How ______ does one pen cost?
explanation_steps: pens → many; cost → much.

textbook_ref.topic: Quantity words (some, any, much, many, too, enough)
textbook_ref.rule: some = an amount with plural or uncountable nouns; too = more than is good; very = a lot; enough = as much as needed.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 148, 274–276; English Grade 8, Units 6–7

additional_textbook_refs.rule: Question word + auxiliary + subject + verb (Why did you travel?). Short answers repeat the auxiliary: Yes, you can.

questions.stem: We will receive our National Examination results ______ August.
explanation_steps: With months we use “in”: in August.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 12; English Grade 8, p. 31, 181.
questions.explain_simple: Months take “in”: in August.
tips: in + month/year; on + date/day; at + clock time.

similar_questions.stem: School starts ______ September.
explanation_steps: month → in.

textbook_ref.rule: Travel: by car/bus/plane; time: at 5 o'clock, on Monday, in June; place: in, on, under, between, next to.

questions.stem: Do you like swimming ______ basketball?
explanation_steps: If the question asks the listener to choose one sport, we use “or”.
But this is a Yes/No question (Do you like …?), so “swimming and basketball” (both) is also correct English.
“but” is wrong. A “or” is the usual choice; D “A and B” is also defensible.
Textbook: English Grade 8, p. 30, 68, 82, 98–99.
questions.explain_simple: We ask about a choice with “or”. (“and” is also possible here.)
tips: or = choice between two things.

similar_questions.stem: Would you like tea ______ coffee? – Tea, please.
explanation_steps: The answer picks one → or.

textbook_ref.rule: because + reason; so that + purpose; but/however + contrast; and + addition; so + result.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 30, 68, 82, 98–99

questions.review_flag: Two defensible answers: A ‘or’ (choice) and D ‘A and B’ – in a yes/no question ‘Do you like swimming and basketball?’ is also correct. Keyed A, D accepted. Teacher decision.

questions.stem: Which pair of words is not correct?
explanation_steps: The plural of leaf is leaves (f → ves), like knife → knives, half → halves.
roof → roofs is an exception and is correct.
Textbook: English Grade 8, p. 72–95 (spelling: doubling letters, dropping 'e').
questions.explain_simple: leaf → leaves, not leafs.
tips: Most -f/-fe words → -ves (leaves, wives); roof → roofs is an exception.

similar_questions.stem: Which plural is wrong?
explanation_steps: wolf → wolves.

textbook_ref.rule: Learn the spelling of common words; the sound /s/ at the end of a word is often spelt -ce (justice, office).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 72–95 (spelling: doubling letters, dropping 'e')

questions.stem: Next year I ______ to Massawa to celebrate the 25th Anniversary of Fenkil Operation.
explanation_steps: “Next year” is the future → will + base verb.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 20, 175.
questions.explain_simple: Next year = future → will travel.
tips: next week/month/year → will.

similar_questions.stem: Tomorrow we ______ our grandmother.
explanation_steps: will visit.

textbook_ref.rule: Future: will + base verb (I will go) or am/is/are going to + base verb.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 20, 175

questions.stem: In which word is the last consonant not doubled before adding “ed” or “ing”?
explanation_steps: hit → hitting, shut → shutting, admit → admitted (the stress is on the last part: ad-MIT).
visit → visited, visiting: the stress is on the first part (VI-sit), so the t is not doubled.
Textbook: English Grade 8, p. 72–95 (spelling: doubling letters, dropping 'e').
questions.explain_simple: visit → visited (one t). The others double: hitting, admitted, shutting.
tips: Double the last letter in short words (hit – hitting) and when the stress is at the end (ad-MIT).

similar_questions.stem: Which word doubles the last letter before -ing?
explanation_steps: stop → stopping.

textbook_ref.rule: Learn the spelling of common words; the sound /s/ at the end of a word is often spelt -ce (justice, office).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 72–95 (spelling: doubling letters, dropping 'e')

questions.stem: Zeineb is 25 years old and Selam is 29 years old. Which sentence is not true about Zeineb and Selam?

options.C: Zeineb is not as old as Selam.

explanation_steps: Selam (29) is older than Zeineb (25).
So “Selam is younger than Zeineb” is not true.

questions.explain_simple: Selam is 29, so she is older. A is not true.

similar_questions.stem: Ali is 12 and Omar is 15. Which is NOT true?

options.D: Ali is not as old as Omar.

questions.stem: As blackboard is to classroom, ______ is to kitchen.
explanation_steps: A blackboard is a thing we find in a classroom.
A pan is a thing we find (and use) in a kitchen.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227.
questions.explain_simple: Blackboard – classroom; pan – kitchen.
tips: Find the link in the first pair, then use it again.

similar_questions.stem: As bed is to bedroom, ______ is to classroom.
explanation_steps: a desk is in a classroom.

questions.stem: The man said, “I am watching the match between Red Sea and Adulis.” Which of the following is the correct indirect speech form?

options.A: The man said that he is watching the match between Red Sea and Adulis.
options.B: The man said that I was watching the match between Red Sea and Adulis.
options.C: The man said that I am watching the match between Red Sea and Adulis.
options.D: The man said that he was watching the match between Red Sea and Adulis.

explanation_steps: I → he (the man).
am watching → was watching (tense moves back).
Textbook: English Grade 8, p. 151, 174–175.
questions.explain_simple: “I am” becomes “he was”.
tips: Reported speech: I → he/she; am/is → was.

similar_questions.stem: The girl said, “I am reading.” Indirect speech:

options.A: The girl said that she was reading.
options.B: The girl said that I was reading.
options.C: The girl said she is read.
options.D: The girl said I am reading.

explanation_steps: I → she, am → was.

textbook_ref.rule: In reported speech after 'said', change the pronoun (I → he/she) and move the tense back (am → was, will → would).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 151, 174–175

questions.stem: When the rain ______, the children were playing basketball.
explanation_steps: The long action is in the past continuous (were playing).
The short action that happens in the middle is past simple: started.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 72; English Grade 8, p. 7.
questions.explain_simple: Short action in the past → started.
tips: When + past simple, … past continuous.

similar_questions.stem: When the teacher ______, the students were talking.
explanation_steps: came.

textbook_ref.rule: Past simple: verb-ed or irregular past form; questions and negatives use did + base verb (Did he call?).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 72; English Grade 8, p. 7

additional_textbook_refs.rule: Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing; it shows an action that was going on at a time in the past.

questions.stem: My grandfather ______ ten years ago at the age of ninety five.
explanation_steps: “ten years ago” → past simple.
“die” is not used in the passive: died (not “was died”).
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 72; English Grade 8, p. 7.
questions.explain_simple: Ten years ago → died.
tips: ago → past simple.

similar_questions.stem: The old tree ______ last year.
explanation_steps: last year → died.

textbook_ref.rule: Past simple: verb-ed or irregular past form; questions and negatives use did + base verb (Did he call?).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 72; English Grade 8, p. 7

questions.stem: I went to visit my uncle’s shop but ______ was closed.

similar_questions.stem: I wanted to read the book, but ______ was lost.

textbook_ref.rule: Use an object pronoun (me, him, her, us, them) after a verb or preposition; possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs) replace a noun.

questions.explain_simple: It adds another good point → moreover.
tips: moreover = also, in addition.

similar_questions.stem: He is a good singer; ______, he plays the guitar.
explanation_steps: adding → moreover.

textbook_ref.rule: because + reason; so that + purpose; but/however + contrast; and + addition; so + result.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 30, 68, 82, 98–99

questions.stem: The driver repaired the car ______.
explanation_steps: We do not know if the driver is a man or a woman.
So “himself” and “herself” are both possible → A and C. “itself” is for things.
Textbook: English Grade 8, p. 56, 112.
questions.explain_simple: A driver can be a man or a woman. So himself or herself.
tips: No clue about man or woman? both himself and herself fit.

similar_questions.stem: The nurse washed the baby ______.
explanation_steps: A nurse can be a woman or a man.

textbook_ref.rule: Reflexive pronouns show that the subject and the object are the same person: you (plural) → yourselves.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 56, 112

questions.review_flag: Same design as Q12: ‘driver’ can be either sex, so D ‘A and C’ (himself/herself) is taken as intended; A ‘himself’ alone is the traditional answer. Teacher decision.

questions.stem: ______ your aunt have children?
explanation_steps: your aunt = she → Does + base verb (have).
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 57; English Grade 8, p. 7.
questions.explain_simple: Aunt = she → Does.
tips: Does + he/she/it + base verb.

similar_questions.stem: ______ your brother play football?
explanation_steps: Does.

textbook_ref.rule: Present simple: he/she/it takes -s (he watches); questions and negatives use do/does + base verb (Does he help?).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 57; English Grade 8, p. 7

additional_textbook_refs.rule: Question word + auxiliary + subject + verb (Why did you travel?). Short answers repeat the auxiliary: Yes, you can.

questions.stem: All students ______ wear their school uniforms during the examination.
explanation_steps: This is a rule → must.
“has to” is wrong with a plural subject (students have to). “must to” is wrong.
“may” means permission, not a rule.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 167–168, 187; English Grade 8, Unit 3 (p. 46–71).
questions.explain_simple: It is a rule: students must wear uniforms.
tips: must + base verb (no to).

similar_questions.stem: Drivers ______ stop at a red light.
explanation_steps: must.

textbook_ref.topic: Modals (must, should, have to, can, may, might)
textbook_ref.rule: Modal verbs (must, should, can, may, might, will) are followed by the base verb without 'to'; have to / ought to keep 'to'.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 167–168, 187; English Grade 8, Unit 3 (p. 46–71)

additional_textbook_refs.rule: A singular subject takes a singular verb (is, has, goes); a plural subject takes a plural verb (are, have, go).

questions.stem: Has she completed her middle school education?
explanation_steps: “Has she …?” → Yes, she has / No, she hasn’t.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 100–101.
questions.explain_simple: “Has she …?” → “Yes, she has.”
tips: Short answer repeats has/hasn’t.

similar_questions.stem: Have you eaten?
explanation_steps: Yes, I have.

textbook_ref.rule: Question word + auxiliary + subject + verb (Why did you travel?). Short answers repeat the auxiliary: Yes, you can.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 100–101

additional_textbook_refs.rule: Present perfect = have/has + past participle (he has taken). Use has with he/she/it and one person.
additional_textbook_refs.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 150; English Grade 8, p. 42, 157

questions.stem: I will not go to the cinema if it ______.
explanation_steps: First conditional: … will …, if + present simple.
it → rains.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 161; English Grade 8, p. 34, 129.
questions.explain_simple: if it rains (present simple with -s).
tips: In the if-part use the present simple, not will.

similar_questions.stem: We will stay at home if it ______ cold.
explanation_steps: if + present.

textbook_ref.rule: First conditional: If + present simple, will + base verb. Zero conditional (always true): If + present, present. Second: If + past, would + base verb.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 161; English Grade 8, p. 34, 129

additional_textbook_refs.rule: A singular subject takes a singular verb (is, has, goes); a plural subject takes a plural verb (are, have, go).

questions.stem: What is American wolf’s favourite food?
explanation_steps: American wolf column, Food row: rubbish and fish.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: The American wolf eats rubbish and fish.
tips: Column (which wolf) + row (which fact).

similar_questions.stem: What does the European wolf eat?
explanation_steps: small animals.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

questions.stem: Which wolves have the same length of tail?
explanation_steps: Tails: European 40 cm, American 35 cm, Australian 35 cm.
American and Australian are the same (35 cm).
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: American and Australian wolves both have 35 cm tails.
tips: Look for equal numbers in one row.

similar_questions.stem: Which wolf is the heaviest?
explanation_steps: 40 kg.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

questions.stem: ______ is taller than American wolf. It is also heavier than Australian wolf.
explanation_steps: European: 80 cm > 50 cm (taller than American) and 40 kg > 20 kg (heavier than Australian) → yes.
Australian is taller than American, but it cannot be heavier than itself. So only A.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: Only the European wolf is both taller than the American wolf and heavier than the Australian wolf.
tips: Both sentences must be true for the answer.

similar_questions.stem: ______ is shorter than the Australian wolf.
explanation_steps: 50 cm < 55 cm.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

additional_textbook_refs.rule: Long adjectives: more ... than / the most ...; short adjectives: -er than / the -est. 'not as ... as' means 'less ... than'.
additional_textbook_refs.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 58; English Grade 7, p. 16, 124; English Grade 8, p. 109

questions.stem: The wolf with the longest tail is ______.
explanation_steps: Tails: 40 cm (European) is the longest.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: The European wolf has the longest tail (40 cm).
tips: longest = biggest number in the tail row.

similar_questions.stem: The lightest wolf is ______.
explanation_steps: 16 kg.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

additional_textbook_refs.rule: Long adjectives: more ... than / the most ...; short adjectives: -er than / the -est. 'not as ... as' means 'less ... than'.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is false about Australian wolf?

options.A: It eats animals as big as kangaroo and sheep.
options.B: Its tail is as long as American wolf’s.
options.C: It is heavier than American wolf.
options.D: It is taller than European wolf.

explanation_steps: A true (food), B true (35 = 35), C true (20 > 16).
D false: 55 cm is shorter than 80 cm.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: The Australian wolf (55 cm) is shorter than the European wolf (80 cm).
tips: For “false”, test every sentence.

similar_questions.stem: Which is false about the European wolf?

options.C: It is lighter than the American wolf.

explanation_steps: 40 kg is heavier than 16 kg.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is true?

options.A: European wolf is lighter than American wolf.
options.B: American wolf is heavier than Australian wolf.
options.C: Australian wolf is lighter than European wolf.
options.D: European wolf is the lightest of the three.

explanation_steps: Weights: European 40, American 16, Australian 20.
C: 20 < 40 → true. The others are false.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: Australian (20 kg) is lighter than European (40 kg).
tips: lighter = smaller weight.

similar_questions.stem: Which is true?

options.A: The American wolf is the tallest.
options.B: The European wolf is the tallest.
options.C: The Australian wolf is the shortest.

explanation_steps: 80 cm.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

questions.stem: What are dolphins?

options.B: They don’t have lungs to breathe with.
options.C: Like all fish, they can feed their young with milk from their mothers’ body.

explanation_steps: First sentence: “Dolphins are not fish, but warm blooded mammals.”
Textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories).
questions.explain_simple: The text says dolphins are warm blooded mammals.
tips: The first sentence often gives the main fact.

similar_questions.stem: How do dolphins feed their young?
explanation_steps: Mammals feed their young with milk.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the part of the text with the same words as the question; read that sentence carefully.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories)

questions.stem: Dolphins are almost different from all land animals in ______ and ______.

options.A: the size of their brain and their age
options.B: the size of their brain and the language they use
options.C: their living in groups and the language they use each other

explanation_steps: “But dolphins are very different from almost all land animals. Their brain is nearly the same size as our own, and they live a long time.”
So the differences are brain size and long life (age). Language and groups make them LIKE bees and birds, so B and C are wrong.
Textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories).
questions.explain_simple: They are different in brain size and long life.
tips: Read the sentences right after “different from”.

similar_questions.stem: In what way are dolphins like bees and birds?

options.B: They live in groups and have their own language.

explanation_steps: “In this they are like other animals, such as bees and birds.”

textbook_ref.rule: Find the part of the text with the same words as the question; read that sentence carefully.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories)

questions.review_flag: Wording in the stem: ‘almost different from all land animals’ is a mix-up of ‘different from almost all land animals’. The answer is not affected.

questions.stem: Who does “They” (line 4) refer to?
explanation_steps: “Dolphins live in groups, and speak to each other … In this they are like other animals.”
“they” = dolphins.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 7–8 (pronouns).
questions.explain_simple: “They” means dolphins.
tips: The pronoun usually refers to the subject of the sentence before.

similar_questions.stem: “Bees make honey. They live in groups.” ‘They’ refers to:
explanation_steps: bees.

textbook_ref.topic: Reference words (he, she, it, them, this)
textbook_ref.rule: A pronoun (he, it, them, this) stands for a noun that came before it; read the sentences before it.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 7–8 (pronouns)

questions.stem: Which of the following is true?

options.A: The relationship between dolphins and human beings started long ago.
options.B: Their long and beak form nose helps dolphins to be strong at smelling.
options.C: Dolphins are very kind to other fishes hence they never eat fish.

explanation_steps: “for thousands of years there have been stories about the dolphin and its friendship with people.” → A true.
B false: “it has no sense of smell”. C false: “it eats fish”.
Textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons.
questions.explain_simple: People and dolphins have been friends for thousands of years.
tips: “thousands of years” = long ago.

similar_questions.stem: Which is true?

options.A: Dolphins have no sense of smell.

explanation_steps: “it has no sense of smell”.

textbook_ref.rule: A 'true' statement must agree with the text in every part; the text may say it in other words.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons

questions.stem: Sound helps dolphins ______

options.B: to talk to each other and find food
options.C: to smell the animals they want to eat

explanation_steps: “dolphins use sounds to help them find their way. They make these sounds to talk to each other and to help them find food.”
So both A and B are true → D.
Textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories).
questions.explain_simple: Sounds help them find their way, talk and find food. A and B.
tips: If two options are both in the text, choose “A and B”.

similar_questions.stem: Dolphins receive sounds with:

options.B: the lower part of the mouth (the jaw)

explanation_steps: “… but the lower part of the mouth called the jaw.”

textbook_ref.rule: Find the part of the text with the same words as the question; read that sentence carefully.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories)

questions.stem: What did Pliny write about?

options.A: He wrote the story of dolphins in the west coast of Africa.
options.B: He wrote about the way dolphins helped fishermen catch fish.
options.C: He wrote about the history of Romans in 70 BCE.
options.D: He wrote about all animals in 70 BCE.

explanation_steps: “Pliny, the Roman writer, wrote about the way dolphins helped fishermen catch fish.”
Textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories).
questions.explain_simple: Pliny wrote how dolphins helped fishermen.
tips: Find the name in the text and read that sentence.

similar_questions.stem: When did Pliny write about dolphins?
explanation_steps: “In about 70 BCE”.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the part of the text with the same words as the question; read that sentence carefully.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories)

questions.stem: What does “the same thing” (line 18) refer to?

options.A: people who wrote about dolphins of Africa
options.C: dolphins which help fishermen catch fish

explanation_steps: The sentence before says dolphins helped fishermen catch fish.
“Today, there are stories about the same thing” = dolphins helping fishermen.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 7–8 (pronouns).
questions.explain_simple: “The same thing” = dolphins helping fishermen catch fish.
tips: Look back at the sentence before.

similar_questions.stem: “Ali likes football. His brother likes the same thing.” ‘the same thing’ =
explanation_steps: football.

textbook_ref.topic: Reference words (he, she, it, them, this)
textbook_ref.rule: A pronoun (he, it, them, this) stands for a noun that came before it; read the sentences before it.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 7–8 (pronouns)

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is false?

options.A: The people of Eritrea don’t do any thing to show the love of Dolphins.
options.B: Many countries have passed a law against the killing of Dolphins.
options.C: The people of Eritrea love dolphins and hence take care of them.
options.D: In our country, the name ‘Abu Salama’ is given to dolphins for they are peaceful animals.

explanation_steps: Eritreans name hotels and shops after dolphins and put their pictures on walls. So A is false.
B, C, D agree with the text.
Textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons.
questions.explain_simple: Eritreans show their love (names, pictures). So A is false.
tips: “false” = the one that disagrees with the text.

similar_questions.stem: Why do people call dolphins ‘Abu Salama’?
explanation_steps: “to show that they are peaceful animals”.

textbook_ref.rule: A 'true' statement must agree with the text in every part; the text may say it in other words.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons

questions.stem: What does “decorated” (line 26) mean?

options.A: to love and take care of someone
options.D: to make walls clear from pictures

explanation_steps: “We also decorate our walls with pictures of dolphins.” Pictures make walls look nicer.
decorate = to make something more attractive.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227.
questions.explain_simple: We put pictures on walls to make them beautiful. That is “decorate”.
tips: Put the meaning in the sentence and check it makes sense.

similar_questions.stem: We decorated the classroom with flowers. ‘Decorated’ means:
explanation_steps: made more beautiful.

textbook_ref.rule: Put each option in place of the word; the one that keeps the meaning of the sentence is correct.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227

questions.review_flag: The stem says ‘decorated’, but the passage (line 26) prints ‘decorate’. Same word; answer not affected.

questions.stem: A good title for the passage could be:
explanation_steps: The whole passage describes dolphins: mammals (not fish), their life, and people.
A is wrong (dolphins are not fish). C and D are only one small part.
B is the best of the four.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 10 (p. 199–220).
questions.explain_simple: The text is about dolphins, which are not fish.
tips: Reject titles that talk about a small part only.

similar_questions.stem: A text describes camels: how they live in the desert, what they eat and how people use them. Best title:
explanation_steps: It covers the whole text.

textbook_ref.rule: The best title covers the whole text, not only one part.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 10 (p. 199–220)
